findings.paper_title: Corporate Finance and Performance Report Q4 2025-26
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creating resource backfill requirements; £1.7M reserve committed with further staffing pressures anticipated
findings.detail: The council faces transition to unitary authority in April 2028. LGR budget of £1M for 2025/26 saw £774K spent with £226K carried forward. Total LGR Reserve now £1.7M, of which £750K is pre-committed to staffing for the programme team, HR, Communications and Legal over the transition period. Management acknowledges potential need for staff backfill 'to ensure continuation of service provision' and sets up monitoring process for resourcing impacts.
findings.matters: A structural reorganisation event creates both direct costs and indirect service delivery risk if backfill is required; pre-commitment of 44% of the LGR reserve leaves limited buffer for unanticipated transition costs.
findings.figures: LGR Reserve 2025/26: £1.7M total; pre-committed staffing: £750K; remaining buffer: £950K
findings.quote: There is potential for to be a requirement to backfill staff working directly on the project to ensure continuation of service provision. It is anticipated that pressures arising from such activity will be funded from the LGR Reserve where they cannot be managed within the service.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Finance and Performance Report Q4 2025-26
findings.headline: One Horton Heath capital project significantly reprofiled with slippage into future years
findings.detail: A material capital scheme slipped in 2025/26 with expenditure reprofiled into future years. The paper notes 'reduced capital expenditure in the year relating to One Horton Heath, as reported in previous quarters'. Section 106 payment obligations were delayed, with slippage 'predominantly related to the reprofiling of the One Horton Heath project'. This is a council-owned housing scheme that has been a focus of cabinet attention.
findings.matters: Slippage on a major council-owned development scheme signals either market conditions (housing demand weakness) or project delivery risk; impacts capital financing profile and debt repayment assumptions.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure 2025/26: £44M total; significant portion of slippage related to One Horton Heath
findings.quote: Slippage on the Community Investment Programme in 2025/26 predominantly related to the reprofiling of the One Horton Heath project, with the impact being that payments for Section 106 obligations needed to be made later than initially envisaged.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Finance and Performance Report Q4 2025-26
findings.headline: Statutory compliance remediation required unplanned spend of £438K across operational and housing assets
findings.detail: A comprehensive statutory compliance review identified fire, electrical, and safety regulation failures. Operational property assets required £185K immediate remediation to meet Fire Safety Order 2005, Gas Safety Regulation 1998, HSAWA, Building Regulations, Electricity at Work Regulations, and Lifting Equipment Regulations. Housing portfolio required additional £253K for fire/electrical safety and damp/mould remediation to comply with Awaab's law. These were unplanned costs triggered by the review.
findings.matters: Unplanned compliance spend of £438K indicates prior control deficiency and creates uncertainty about whether full compliance picture is now visible; regulatory failures could trigger enforcement action.
findings.figures: Operational property remediation: £185K; housing portfolio compliance: £253K; total: £438K
findings.quote: A comprehensive statutory compliance review across the year identified improvements for fire and electrical safety across the Council's operational property portfolio. There were remediation works required to remove unforeseen non-compliance with a spend of £185,000

findings.paper_title: Corporate Finance and Performance Report Q4 2025-26
findings.headline: Housing Benefit subsidy deficit worsening with no control over costs; trend expected to deteriorate further
findings.detail: Housing Benefit and Council Tax Support overspent by £307K in 2025/26 on demand-led services. The council identifies a structural problem: Universal Credit migration has shifted case mix toward high-cost rent officer determination cases that attract minimal subsidy. Individual claims can exceed £50K per year with only £10K subsidy. The finance report explicitly states this trend is expected to worsen and will require further budget growth.
findings.matters: A growing, uncontrollable demand-led pressure with explicit expectation of deterioration signals structural budget risk that cannot be managed through service efficiency.
findings.figures: Housing Benefit overspend 2025/26: £307K; individual claims: up to £50K/year with £10K subsidy
findings.quote: This trend of increasingly complex and costly cases is expected to worsen in future years and likely to require further growth.

findings.paper_title: Corporate Finance and Performance Report Q4 2025-26
findings.headline: Investment Property Reserve will be exhausted in 2027/28, forcing £1.4M General Fund impact
findings.detail: The council's Investment Property Reserve is being drawn down faster than planned due to void costs and lease renewal incentives. A net draw of £3.6M occurred in 2025/26 (£2.8M budgeted). Forecast balances show the reserve declining from £3.162M (2025/26) to £452K (2026/27) to £0 (2027/28), at which point a £1.4M annual cost will hit the General Fund. The primary driver is Wessex House closure in February 2025 and incentives needed to secure lease renewals.
findings.matters: A council burning through a major asset reserve within 18 months signals deteriorating income-generating capacity and upcoming structural deficit pressures, which directly affects debt serviceability.
findings.figures: Investment Property Reserve: £3.162M (2025/26), £452K (2026/27), £0 (2027/28); General Fund impact 2027/28: £1.4M; net draw 2025/26: £3.6M (vs £2.8M budgeted)
findings.quote: This shows that the Investment Property Reserve is forecast to be exhausted during 2027/28 with future costs needing to be borne by the General Fund.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Treasury Management Outturn Position
findings.headline: Pooled property fund accounting override expires 2029 with no indication it will be renewed
findings.detail: The council holds £8.6m in strategic pooled property funds whose accounting treatment relies on a statutory override expiring 31 March 2029. The paper states commentary "suggests it will not" be extended beyond that date. Commercial property valuations "became more uncertain towards the end of the period". The council notes it will "discuss with Arlingclose the implications for the investment strategy."
findings.matters: If the override lapses, the council loses smoothed accounting for pooled fund volatility and will be forced to recognize annual valuation swings through the P&L, creating potential asset write-downs and accounting surprises.
findings.figures: £8.6m in pooled property funds, override expires 31 March 2029
findings.quote: The override has been extended until 31st March 2029, but no other changes have been made; whether the override will be extended beyond this date is unknown but commentary to the consultation outcome suggests it will not.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Treasury Management Outturn Position
findings.headline: Short-term borrowing surged £44.8m to 44% of portfolio as new rates jumped to 5.0%-7.0%
findings.detail: Short-term borrowing rose from £235.3m to £280.1m (a 19% increase), while long-term fell £10m. The council's spot rates for new LA-to-LA borrowing at year-end reached 5.0%-7.0%, up sharply from 4.0%-4.5% for most of the year, though the existing short-term book averages 3.64%. At 44%, short-term now sits near the 50% upper maturity limit.
findings.matters: Growing short-term exposure combined with year-end rate spikes signals rising refinancing risk. When this £280m portfolio rolls, the council may be forced to issue at 5-7% rather than today's blended 2.95%, materially raising debt service costs.
findings.figures: Short-term borrowing £280.092m (up £44.776m), average rate 3.64%, spot rates 5.0%-7.0% at year-end, maturity 44% under 12 months (limit 50%), total borrowing weighted average 2.95%
findings.quote: The cost of short-term borrowing from other local authorities has been similar to or a little above Base Rate for most of the period, with interest rates between 4.0% and 4.5%. However, as is commonly seen, rates rose higher towards the end of the financial year, with rates of 5.0% - 7.0% being seen.

findings.paper_title: Eastleigh - Internal Audit Annual Conclusion 2025 -26
findings.headline: Information Governance audit found significant GDPR compliance weaknesses including gaps in breach management and training
findings.detail: Despite established policies and a Data Protection Officer, audit found outdated policies, gaps in training compliance and monitoring, weaknesses in data breach management and recording, limited data retention oversight, no formal destruction policy, and insufficient use of trend analysis.
findings.matters: GDPR non-compliance creates regulatory and financial risk; data governance weaknesses affect data security and accountability
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Significant weaknesses remain across the control framework, including outdated policies, gaps in training compliance and monitoring, and weaknesses in the management and recording of data breaches. In addition, there is limited oversight of data retention, no formal destruction policy, and insufficient use of trend analysis to support organisational learning.

findings.paper_title: Eastleigh - Internal Audit Annual Conclusion 2025 -26
findings.headline: Multiple service areas received 'Limited' assurance ratings indicating control weaknesses across procurement and governance
findings.detail: Seven audits received 'Limited' assurance across Housing Repairs and Maintenance, Tree Maintenance, Information Governance, Business Continuity, Software Licensing, Cyber Awareness and One Horton Heath. Common themes include non-compliance with Contract Standing Orders, limited contractor oversight, informal governance processes, data integrity gaps, and incomplete policy frameworks.
findings.matters: Systemic control weaknesses across multiple service areas suggest wider governance and compliance risk; gaps in contractor management increase procurement risk and potential for fraud
findings.figures: 7 audits with 'Limited' assurance rating out of reviews with defined ratings
findings.quote: A number of audits identified weaknesses in procurement and contractor arrangements, including non-compliance with internal processes, limited transparency in tendering, and a lack of formal performance monitoring.

findings.paper_title: Eastleigh - Internal Audit Annual Conclusion 2025 -26
findings.headline: Statutory Checks on Council Estate received 'No' assurance rating due to fundamental control weaknesses
findings.detail: The audit identified fundamental weaknesses in governance and control for statutory compliance checks across the council's non-residential estate, including absence of a complete asset register, unclear allocation of responsibilities, lack of overarching policy framework, underdeveloped monitoring and reporting, reliance on manual processes, instances of overdue checks, missing evidence, and gaps in contractor assurance.
findings.matters: Failure in statutory compliance (e.g. fire safety, electrical safety) creates legal liability and reputational risk; incomplete asset register limits financial visibility
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The audit identified fundamental weaknesses, including the absence of a complete asset register, unclear allocation of responsibilities, and a lack of an overarching policy framework for statutory compliance. Governance, monitoring and reporting arrangements are underdeveloped, with reliance on manual processes and limited formal oversight. Instances of overdue checks and missing evidence were identified, alongside gaps in contractor assurance and staff competency arrangements.

findings.paper_title: Eastleigh - Internal Audit Annual Conclusion 2025 -26
findings.headline: One Horton Heath capital programme showing slippage and cost pressure risks despite improved governance
findings.detail: The audit found governance arrangements have improved with a Programme Board in place, but significant risks remain including slower than planned progress, incomplete programme planning, and weaknesses in procurement consistency. Delays in tendering and contractor performance variability increase risk of cost pressures and programme slippage.
findings.matters: Capital programme overruns directly impact council finances and borrowing requirements; slippage affects service delivery timelines
findings.figures: None specific to cost variance provided
findings.quote: Significant risks remain, including slower than planned progress, incomplete programme planning, and weaknesses in procurement consistency and contingency planning. Delays in tendering and variability in contractor performance increase the risk of cost pressures and programme slippage.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement App 1
findings.headline: External audit opinion on 2025/26 accounts not yet available at governance statement publication
findings.detail: The council's external auditor (EY) had not provided an audit opinion on the 2025/26 accounts when this governance statement was published. The council acknowledges it may need to amend the AGS pending audit completion and notes the accounts remain unaudited.
findings.matters: Audited financial statements provide independent assurance of the council's financial position. Publishing governance statements before audit completion is procedurally compliant but leaves the financial position unverified by external auditors at publication date.
findings.figures: 2025/26 accounts unaudited at time of statement publication
findings.quote: At the time of drafting this report, our external auditor (EY) is not yet able to provide an opinion on the accounts for 2025/26... As the accounts remain unaudited, we may need to consider if changes are necessary to the AGS in the period leading up to the finalisation of that audit.

findings.paper_title: 25 Eastleigh Borough Council - Auditor's Annual Report - 7 April 2026
findings.headline: Material misstatements in accounts; volume and quality of errors rated ineffective; delays in providing asset valuation evidence
findings.detail: EY detected a 'large number of material misstatements' in the Statement of Accounts, with specific issues: (1) Misstatements in Short-Term Creditors balance (no assurance provided); (2) REFCUS (Revenue Expenditure Funded by Capital Under Statute) understatement £0.073m; (3) IFRS 16 lease liability/right-of-use-asset errors £0.252m; (4) One Horton Heath costs overstatement £0.3m. Two control environment areas rated 'Ineffective': 'Volume and value of identified misstatements' and 'Volume of misstatements in disclosure'. Significant delays experienced in provision of PPE and Investment Property valuation evidence, resulting in EY flagging scale fee variation.
findings.matters: Material misstatements across multiple account areas, combined with control environment rated ineffective, indicate financial reporting cannot be relied upon. No assurance over creditors (operational liabilities) is particularly concerning.
findings.figures: REFCUS understatement £0.073m; IFRS 16 errors £0.252m; One Horton Heath overstatement £0.3m; scale fee variations flagged
findings.quote: A large number of material misstatements were detected as a result of our work. The misstatements identified included those within the Short-Term Creditors significant account. As a result of these misstatements, we are unable to conclude on the completeness or accuracy of the creditors balance held at 31 March 2024

findings.paper_title: 25 Eastleigh Borough Council - Auditor's Annual Report - 7 April 2026
findings.headline: Cumulative budget gap of £18 million by 2028/29; council relying on £19 million Earmarked Reserve transfer to avoid 2024/25 deficit
findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Strategy identifies an £18.0 million cumulative budget gap across 2025/26 to 2028/29. Savings identified total only £7.311 million, leaving £11.176 million unresolved. For 2024/25, the council recorded a £15.842 million underspend against the Rolling Budget, but this was only achieved through a £19.005 million transfer from Earmarked Reserves. EY notes: 'Had this transfer not taken place, or if the Council did not have sufficient reserves for this transfer, the Council's overall position would show a £3.163 million deficit.' This indicates structural overspend masked by reserve depletion.
findings.matters: Structural deficit (£3.163m operational deficit before reserve transfers) is unsustainable. Reliance on reserves suggests inability to live within tax/grant income. Reserves will deplete if borrowing does not service development returns.
findings.figures: Budget gap £18.0m cumulative 2025/26-2028/29; Earmarked Reserve transfer £19.005m in 2024/25; structural deficit £3.163m
findings.quote: Had this transfer not taken place, or if the Council did not have sufficient reserves for this transfer, the Council's overall position would show a £3.163 million deficit

findings.paper_title: 25 Eastleigh Borough Council - Auditor's Annual Report - 7 April 2026
findings.headline: Borrowing increased to £585 million with £235.3 million short-term, up £92 million in one year, and DLUHC remains concerned despite lifting Best Value Notice
findings.detail: Total borrowing stood at £585 million as of 31 March 2025, up from £583 million 31 March 2024. Short-term borrowing (expected to mature within 12 months) reached £235.3 million as of 31 March 2025, an increase of £92 million year-on-year. DLUHC lifted its December 2024 Best Value Notice (originally issued 2023) but stated in the expiration letter: 'the Council should continue engaging regularly with the department to provide assurance of the steps being taken to reduce and manage its overall debt.' EY explicitly states concern: 'Council continues to hold a high level of borrowing relative to their revenue spend, with an increasing portion of borrowing held on a short-term basis.'
findings.matters: £235.3m of short-term borrowing maturing within 12 months creates refinancing risk. Continued DLUHC concern suggests systemic debt management issues. Ratio of borrowing to revenue spend indicates limited debt reduction trajectory.
findings.figures: Total borrowing £585m (31 March 2025); short-term borrowing £235.3m; increase in short-term borrowing £92m year-on-year
findings.quote: We remain concerned that the Council therefore continues to a hold a high level of borrowing relative to their revenue spend, with an increasing portion of borrowing held on a short-term basis

findings.paper_title: 25 Eastleigh Borough Council - Auditor's Annual Report - 7 April 2026
findings.headline: One Horton Heath development – £187.1 million cumulative spend with governance and procurement risks, explicitly absent from medium-term financial strategy
findings.detail: The Council has invested £187.1 million to 31 March 2025 in a major housing and commercial property development. £90 million PWLB borrowing was secured in 2023/24 for the delivery phase. EY identified governance and procurement risks as significant risks. The Council has not explicitly mentioned this £187m development in its Medium Term Financial Strategy despite its scale. EY recommended scenario modelling for major capital acquisitions; this recommendation from 2023/24 remains outstanding. A £0.3 million overstatement was identified in development costs.
findings.matters: A £187m development at a council holding £585m total borrowing represents concentration risk. Absence from MTFS suggests governance weakness. Auditor concerns about informed decision-making suggest members may lack full scenario information.
findings.figures: £187.1 million cumulative spend to 31 March 2025; £90 million PWLB borrowing 2023/24; £0.3 million cost overstatement identified
findings.quote: The One Horton Heath (OHH) development is not explicitly mentioned in the MTFS, despite its large scale and potential impact on the Council's finances

findings.paper_title: 25 Eastleigh Borough Council - Auditor's Annual Report - 7 April 2026
findings.headline: Accounts disclaimer of opinion – unable to sign off accounts after cascading audit failures across four years
findings.detail: EY issued a disclaimed opinion on 12 February 2026 because prior-year disclaimers (2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24) mean there is no assurance over opening balances and therefore no assurance over all 2024/25 in-year movements or 2023/24 comparative balances. The audit opinion explicitly states the council cannot demonstrate accounts are free from material and pervasive misstatement. EY assesses it is unlikely full assurance can be restored by 2026/27.
findings.matters: Lenders rely on audited accounts to assess financial position. A four-year disclaimer means no reliable baseline for credit decisions. This signals fundamental accounting control failures.
findings.figures: Disclaimer issued 12 February 2026; cascading from 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24; progress roadmap shows only 'Unqualified opinion' possible 2026/27 at earliest
findings.quote: due to the disclaimers of opinion on the Statement of Accounts in the prior years, we have not been able to complete the detailed audit procedures that would be needed to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to issue an unmodified audit report on the Council's Statement of Accounts for the year ended 31 March 2025

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 2
findings.headline: Capital programme commits council to sustained high borrowing of £800M+ over forecast period, establishing long-term borrower status.
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) is forecast to grow from £623M (2024/25) to £837M (2028/29), driven by a capital programme that requires borrowing to rise to £800M. The council acknowledges 'The Council is expecting to be a long-term borrower,' representing a shift from episodic capital borrowing to structural high-level debt.
findings.matters: Large, sustained capital commitments signal either strong growth plans or significant service infrastructure needs; both require execution. Failure to deliver the programme leaves the council over-borrowed; delivery at higher rates than forecast would strain affordability.
findings.figures: CFR rising from £623M to £837M; external borrowing to £800M; Internal borrowing held at £37M-£38M
findings.quote: The Council has an increasing CFR due to the capital programme, but minimal investments and therefore borrowing will increase up to £800M over the forecast period.

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 2
findings.headline: Council deliberately accepting refinancing risk through short-term borrowing strategy to reduce interest costs.
findings.detail: Rather than locking in long-term fixed rates, the council is pursuing short-term borrowing to capture lower rates expected to fall to 3.25%. The paper explicitly acknowledges this creates 'refinancing risk' that is 'mitigated by the Council's ongoing access to the PWLB funds, and the liquid short term local to local borrowing market, allowing access to refinance borrowing as it becomes repayable.'
findings.matters: This strategy depends on continued access to debt markets at refinancing maturity; any market disruption or loss of access would force the council to refinance at unfavourable terms or draw on limited reserves.
findings.figures: Short-term borrowing assumed at 3.79%; medium/long-term at 4.58%; forecast Bank Rate cut to 3.25%
findings.quote: This strategy should maintain a lower cost of borrowing through the financing of short-term loans but does show the refinancing risk this presents to the Council.

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 2
findings.headline: Usable reserves declining 47% over four years while borrowing grows 37%, reducing financial cushion.
findings.detail: Usable reserves are forecast to fall from £49M (2024/25 actual) to £26M by 2028/29, a reduction of £23M. Over the same period, external borrowing is forecast to rise from £585M to £800M, reaching 771% of remaining reserves by the end of the forecast. This combination reduces the council's financial flexibility to handle unexpected costs or income shortfalls without additional borrowing.
findings.matters: A shrinking reserve buffer combined with rising debt levels constrains a council's ability to manage financial stress or take advantage of unexpected opportunities, increasing lender risk.
findings.figures: Reserves: £49M (2024/25) to £26M (2028/29); External borrowing: £585M (2024/25) to £800M (2028/29); CFR rising to £837M by 2028/29
findings.quote: Less: Usable Reserves (49) (43) (38) (32) (26)

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 1C
findings.headline: Planned use of capital receipts accelerates sharply to £1.788M in 2025/26, drawing down limited pool of £3.252M available
findings.detail: The council plans to deploy £1.788M in capital receipts for Service Improvement and Efficiencies projects in 2025/26, a tenfold increase from £135,603 in 2024/25. With only £3.252M available in total for flexibility and just £121k forecast in new receipts for 2025/26, this acceleration significantly depletes the remaining stock. At this deployment rate, available receipts will be exhausted within 2 years.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand whether the council is substituting finite one-off capital for sustainable revenue savings. If transformation projects fail to deliver promised efficiencies, or if capital receipts are exhausted before savings materialise, the council faces a structural funding gap.
findings.figures: £1,788k approved for 2025/26; £135,603 in 2024/25; £3,252k total available for flexibility; £121k forecast receipts for 2025/26
findings.quote: In 2024/25, £135,603 of flexible use of capital receipts were successfully utilised to achieve savings in the Communications and Neighbourhoods areas.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 26-27
findings.headline: Parking income still not recovered to pre-pandemic levels; £132k annual growth required in 2026/27
findings.detail: Four years after the pandemic, the council's car park income has not returned to pre-pandemic levels. The council is forecasting ongoing growth of £132k required in 2026/27, and included in this a forecast £84k uplift from new charging structures and capital investment. This signals that underlying demand has not recovered and the council is having to restructure pricing and invest in infrastructure to offset structural loss of footfall.
findings.matters: Parking income signals the health of local footfall, town centres, and retail recovery. Persistent shortfalls suggest structural economic challenges in the borough rather than a temporary post-COVID dip, which has implications for the council's ability to sustain discretionary service funding.
findings.figures: £132k annual growth required in 2026/27 to offset unrecovered parking income; £84k expected from pricing changes
findings.quote: use of the Council's Car Parks, and thus the surpluses previously enjoyed, have not fully recovered to pre-pandemic levels. Growth of £354,000 in 2025/26 and £132,000 in 2026/27 is required.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 26-27
findings.headline: Chalcroft Solar Farm income down £142k due to falling export prices; significant asset generating lower returns than forecast
findings.detail: The Chalcroft Solar Farm, a capital investment that generates revenue, has experienced falling export prices reducing income by £142k annually on an ongoing basis. The council notes the farm remains profitable and has fixed the export price for 2026/27, but this signals that a key income-generating asset is exposed to commodity price risk and may not deliver the returns originally planned.
findings.matters: A lender tracking the council's revenue-generating assets needs to understand performance against forecast and whether the council's treasury or investment forecasting has built in adequate contingency for price volatility in renewable energy markets.
findings.figures: £142k ongoing loss of income at Chalcroft Solar Farm due to falling export prices
findings.quote: Falling export prices at Chalcroft Solar Farm have meant the income levels require £142,000 of ongoing growth. The export price has been fixed for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 26-27
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) costs unknown; £1.5m earmarked in reserves but full financial impact not yet quantified
findings.detail: The council is preparing for an unspecified local government reorganisation across Hampshire following a ministerial decision that has not yet been made. The full costs and financing of LGR are unknown. The council has earmarked £1.5m in reserves for 'existing commitments relating to LGR and Asset Transfers' and budgeted £200k in 2026/27 for programme team and external consultants. However, this assumes the council knows its full exposure, which the report explicitly states it does not. A future Cabinet report will be required after the ministerial decision to quantify the real impact.
findings.matters: A material unknown financial liability creates uncertainty around medium-term cash flows and may result in unanticipated costs materialising during the MTFP period. The £1.5m provision may prove inadequate, and any additional LGR costs could be unbudgeted.
findings.figures: £1.5m earmarked in reserves; £200k budgeted in 2026/27 for programme team and consultants; real costs 'not yet known'
findings.quote: With the Council currently awaiting a decision by Ministers about the future structure of local government across Hampshire, the full costs and financing to deliver LGR are not yet known and therefore the Budget for 2026/27 and the MTFP included within this report have been compiled on a 'business as usual' basis.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 26-27
findings.headline: Escalating savings targets of £2.5m by 2028/29 with limited detail on how they will be achieved; report provides no confidence assessment
findings.detail: From 2026/27, the council has introduced new savings targets: £500k in 2026/27, £1m in 2027/28, and £2.5m in 2028/29. The report states these will be achieved through commercial property portfolio returns, reviewing commercial services (Trade Waste), implementing a revised savings programme with LGR partners, and rationalising capital scheme forecasts. However, the document provides no detail on baseline costs, current performance against these services, or how confident the council is in achieving £2.5m of savings three years out. The conclusion states outright that 'The achievement of the new savings target...is important to enable the continued financial stability.'
findings.matters: A lender cannot assess credit quality when the balanced budget depends on savings targets that are not detailed or evidenced. The fact that the council's reserves deplete to £4.959m *only if these targets are met* means a 10-15% slip would breach minimum reserves. Yet the mechanisms are vague and the largest target (£2.5m in 28/29) rests on an external factor — LGR partnership — over which the council has limited control.
findings.quote: The achievement of the new savings target and regular reviews of the assumptions included in the MTFP from 2026/27 is important to enable the continued financial stability of the Council over the MTFP period.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 26-27
findings.headline: Net borrowing forecast at £667m by end of 2026/27; only 60% is fixed rate; council is paying a 0.5% sector premium (£1m per annum) due to local government credit stress
findings.detail: The council will have £667m of net borrowing by the end of 2026/27. Only 60% of this is fixed at an average rate of 2.15%; the remaining 40% is exposed to short-term interest rate movements. The budget includes an additional 0.5% premium on borrowing (adding £1m per annum in costs) specifically because of the sector-wide credit stress — Section 114 notices, Best Value Notices, and funding gaps at other authorities have forced the entire local government sector to pay higher rates. This premium is only forecast until end of 2027/28.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand both the quantum of debt and the refinancing risk. £667m is substantial, and the council is bearing a contingent cost premium that depends on when sector credit conditions normalise. If interest rates remain volatile or sector stress continues beyond 2028, the premium could persist longer.
findings.figures: £667m net borrowing forecast by end 2026/27; 60% fixed at 2.15% average; 40% variable; £1m per annum sector credit premium included until end 2027/28
findings.quote: Net borrowing levels are anticipated to be £667M by the end of 2026/27. As at 31 December 2025, the Council had fixed approximately 60% of its borrowing with the PWLB at a rate averaging 2.15%. It is considered prudent to add a premium to the interest rate forecasts to take account of the current credit negative press that is occurring within the local government sector.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 26-27
findings.headline: Housing Benefit subsidy gap of £420k annually; central government admin grants falling with £208k pressure in 2026/27 alone
findings.detail: The council faces a structural subsidy gap on Housing Benefits of £420k per year due to temporary and exempt accommodation where the government pays a lower subsidy rate than the full cost. Additionally, central government grants to administer the benefit are falling year on year — this creates a £208k budget pressure in 2026/27 against shrinking government support, yet the council must maintain a 'small but resilient team' to manage the caseload and provide flexibility for sickness and leave.
findings.matters: This is a structural funding problem, not a one-off cost. The council cannot control either the subsidy rates central government sets or the composition of its caseload (temporary accommodation). It signals that the subsidy regime is no longer aligned with actual costs, and the gap could widen if temporary accommodation demand grows.
findings.figures: £420k annual subsidy gap; £58k pressure in 2025/26 and £208k in 2026/27 from falling admin grants
findings.quote: The £420,000 gap between Housing Benefit payments and the subsidy received, is due, in the main, to temporary/exempt accommodation for which full subsidy cannot be claimed. Additionally, the grants received to administer Housing Benefit continue to decrease year on year, resulting in a pressure of £58,000 in 2025/26 and £208,000 in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 26-27
findings.headline: Business Rates reset will reduce income by £1.82m in 2026/27
findings.detail: From 2026/27, the government's revaluation of business rates (national rates reset) is forecast to reduce the council's retained income by £1.82m compared to the revised 2025/26 position. This is a permanent loss of central government funding, not a one-off adjustment.
findings.matters: A sudden £1.82m annual loss of income is material to a council's financial sustainability. It represents a reduction in predictable revenue and reduces flexibility to respond to other pressures.
findings.figures: £1.82m reduction in retained business rates from 2026/27 onwards
findings.quote: in line with external advice, it is forecast that from 2026/27 the value of rates will be reset and reduced by £1.82M from the revised 2025/26 position.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 26-27
findings.headline: General fund reserve forecast to fall to £4.959m by 2028/29, a drop of £11.2m in three years, dependent on achieving escalating savings targets
findings.detail: The council's general fund reserve grows slightly to £16.1m in 2026/27 but then falls sharply to £10.6m in 2027/28 and £4.959m in 2028/29. This trajectory assumes the council successfully achieves savings targets of £500k (2026/27), £1m (2027/28), and £2.5m (2028/29). The report explicitly states these savings are 'important to enable the continued financial stability of the Council over the MTFP period', indicating the budget has no cushion if targets slip.
findings.matters: A lender assesses reserve adequacy against minimum requirements and unexpected shocks. A reserve falling to £4.959m (only marginally above the minimum of £1.553m by 2028/29) with no buffer leaves the council vulnerable if savings targets are missed or if unforeseen pressures emerge.
findings.figures: General Fund closing balances: £15.450m (2025/26 revised), £16.130m (2026/27), £10.603m (2027/28), £4.959m (2028/29); minimum required £1.553m (10% of £15.532m GF requirement)
findings.quote: The General Fund Reserve is forecast to exceed the minimum requirement of the higher of £1M or 10% of the Net General Fund Requirement until 2028/29 assuming the savings targets detailed later in this report are achieved.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 26-27
findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio generating major losses from long-term voids; property reserve will be depleted by 2027/28
findings.detail: The council's commercial property portfolio is experiencing significant losses due to major voids and lease delays. In 2026/27 alone, this will require an additional £1.72m to be drawn from the Property Reserve. Despite these assets still contributing a net revenue surplus, the reserve that has been absorbing these losses for years will be completely depleted by 2027/28, after which losses will directly impact the general fund.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can sustain commercial property investments that are consuming reserves at this rate, and what the underlying property issues are — voids suggest either asset quality problems, market positioning, or portfolio management challenges.
findings.figures: £1.62m draw in 2026/27; £1.72m additional cost from major voids and lease events; Property Reserve forecast £5.0m (2025/26) → £1.8m (2026/27) → depleted 2027/28
findings.quote: Despite still contributing a net revenue surplus, delays in lease events and long-term voids evidence that this surplus is no longer able to support the wider service budgets. It is forecast that the Property Reserve will be depleted in 2027/28 and there will be an ongoing impact on the General Fund from that point if major voids are not resolved.

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 3
findings.headline: Commercial income projected to continue declining while reserves deplete
findings.detail: Commercial property income is falling year-on-year (from £21.1m to £19.7m forecast by 2026/27) at the same time that the council's liquidity reserve coverage ratio is worsening (from 50% to 78% of investment income). The income-to-reserves ratio shows increasing pressure: £19.7m income against only £25.1m reserves means any significant income disruption would force difficult choices.
findings.matters: The trend line is negative on both sides of the equation—declining income and depleting reserves—creating cumulative pressure on the council's financial position and its ability to service debt.
findings.quote: Gross Commercial Property Income 2024/25 £21,110k, 2025/26 Forecast £19,919k, 2026/27 Forecast £19,726k

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 3
findings.headline: Property reserve depleted to £760k by 2026/27, down from £5.9m
findings.detail: The earmarked reserve held to cover void costs, rent-free periods, empty rates, and maintenance on commercial properties is being drained from £5.9m to just £760k. This reserve is meant to cushion income loss when tenants leave or maintenance needs arise; at £760k it provides minimal protection.
findings.matters: With voids already at 15% and a void reserve of only £760k, the council has limited capacity to absorb further property underperformance without drawing on general reserves or reducing services.
findings.quote: Investment Property Reserve 2024/25 Actual £5,869k, 2025/26 Forecast £3,970k, 2026/27 Forecast £760k

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 3
findings.headline: Usable reserves forecast to drop 41% from £42.3m to £25.1m in three years
findings.detail: Revenue reserves available to the council are declining sharply, from £42.3m to £25.1m over the three-year forecast. This compresses the council's financial resilience and means less buffer against unexpected costs or income shortfalls.
findings.matters: A shrinking reserve base, combined with dependency on volatile commercial income, reduces the council's ability to absorb shocks or fund unexpected expenditure.
findings.quote: Usable revenue reserves 2024/25 actual £42,301k, 2025/26 forecast £31,474k, 2026/27 forecast £25,087k

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 3
findings.headline: Council structurally dependent on commercial property profit to balance budget
findings.detail: Commercial property income is forecast to account for 29% of gross service expenditure by 2026/27, up from 22% in 2024/25. The council explicitly states it is dependent on this income to achieve a balanced revenue budget. This creates vulnerability if property income falters.
findings.matters: A lender assessing budget sustainability needs to know the council cannot balance its books without commercial property returns; if the portfolio underperforms (as evidenced by rising voids and declining yields), the council faces a structural deficit.
findings.figures: 2024/25 22%, 2025/26 27%, 2026/27 29% of gross service expenditure
findings.quote: The Council is dependent on profit generating investment activity to achieve a balanced revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 3
findings.headline: Commercial property yield declining from 6.42% to 5.53% forecast
findings.detail: The gross yield on the commercial property portfolio is trending downward across the three-year forecast window. This reflects both the general economic headwinds (mentioned: lease term compression from 20-25 years to 5-10 years, rent-free periods and stepped rents) and suggests the portfolio is generating lower returns than historically achieved.
findings.matters: Declining yields, combined with voids and negative security, show the income line the council depends on to balance its budget is under sustained pressure.
findings.quote: Commercial Property Yield 2024/25 Actual 6.42%, 2025/26 Forecast 5.65%, 2026/27 Forecast 5.53%

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 3
findings.headline: Commercial property voids jumped from 2.5% to 15.4% of portfolio in one year
findings.detail: Vacant square footage rose from 30,229 sq feet to 183,457 sq feet between 2024/25 and 2025/26. The council attributes this largely to one asset becoming vacant, but the scale of the increase means the council is not generating expected rental income across a much larger slice of its portfolio.
findings.matters: Voids directly reduce the commercial income the council now depends on for 29% of service expenditure; a 6x increase in vacancies suggests the portfolio is not performing as modelled.
findings.quote: It should be noted that the large increase in void levels from 2024/25 to 2025/26 is predominantly due to one asset in the portfolio becoming vacant.

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 3
findings.headline: Asset valuations £27m underwater against debt outstanding
findings.detail: The council's commercial and housing investments have a security value of negative £27,027k, meaning the outstanding debt of £548.8m exceeds asset valuations of £521.7m. The council expects this to improve through debt repayment, but currently the portfolio provides no equity cushion against falling values or income losses.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether collateral backing council debt is deteriorating; negative security means the council has no asset buffer if property values fall further or yields collapse.
findings.figures: Asset valuations £521,745k, Debt outstanding £548,772k, Security value (£27,027k)
findings.quote: This indicator returns a negative security value, despite the Council's continued prudent provision for the repayment of debt.

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 2B
findings.headline: Net borrowing requirement grows by £66m+ annually, accumulating £214m of new debt over five years
findings.detail: In-year net borrowing requirement rises from £2.3m (2025/26) to £26.3m (2026/27), then accelerates to £55.6m (2026/27), £66.2m (2027/28), and £66.3m (2028/29). Total gross borrowing grows from £585.3m to £799.7m — an addition of £214.4m.
findings.matters: Rapid debt accumulation, combined with high financing cost ratios and depleting reserves, increases refinancing risk and constrains future borrowing headroom
findings.quote: In year borrowing requirement 2,310 26,301 55,567 66,165 66,311

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 2B
findings.headline: Commercial property and housing investments are valued below outstanding debt
findings.detail: The security indicator shows negative figures: (£19.1m) in 2024/25 actual and (£27.0m) in 2025/26 estimate. Negative security means the accounting valuation of assets is less than the debt outstanding against them. This worsens from 2024/25 to 2025/26 and figures are listed as n/a (no data) from 2026/27 onwards.
findings.matters: Underwater commercial investments indicate credit risk; if asset values decline further or yields fall, the council faces potential impairment and loss, constraining reserves and balance sheet strength
findings.quote: Security of Commercial and Housing Investments Investment Strategy (19,112) (27,027) n/a n/a n/a

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 2B
findings.headline: Commercial property investment reserve depletes from £5.9m to zero by 2027/28
findings.detail: The reserve falls from £5.9m (2024/25 actual) to £3.9m (2025/26), then collapses to £760k (2026/27) and reaches zero by 2027/28 and 2028/29. This reserve is meant to cover losses from void properties or maintenance; its depletion leaves no buffer.
findings.matters: Exhaustion of the commercial income buffer removes the council's ability to absorb income shortfalls or unexpected maintenance; this signals reliance on sustained commercial yields or increases refinancing risk
findings.quote: Commercial Property Investments Reserve Levels Capital Strategy 5,869 3,970 760 0 0

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 2B
findings.headline: Financing costs rise to 134–138% of net revenue stream by 2027/28–2028/29
findings.detail: Interest and Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) costs grow from 120% of net annual budget (2026/27) to 138% (2028/29). This means the council's debt servicing costs alone exceed its entire net revenue budget by over 30%, creating acute affordability pressure.
findings.matters: Financing costs above 100% of revenue is a major stress indicator; lenders assess sustainability of debt service and this trajectory signals deteriorating headroom
findings.quote: Proportion of financing costs to net revenue stream Capital Strategy 128% 122% 120% 134% 138%

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 2B
findings.headline: Capital expenditure more than doubles in 2026/27, then stays elevated through 2027/28
findings.detail: Annual capital spend jumps from £48.9m (2025/26 estimate) to £109.1m (2026/27), then £125.8m (2027/28), before dropping back to £83.9m (2028/29). This represents a 123% increase year-on-year and signals a major shift in the council's capital programme timing and scale.
findings.matters: Material increase in capital commitments requires corresponding borrowing and constrains affordability; lenders need to understand what is driving this expansion and how it will be financed
findings.quote: Total Annual Capital Expenditure Capital Strategy 36,475 48,943 109,119 125,844 83,946

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 2A
findings.headline: Scale of housing developments requires bespoke MRP treatment distinct from other capital to protect core service liquidity
findings.detail: The council is moving to a housing-specific annuity method 'in order to reflect the scale and financial profile of the Council's housing developments.' The policy explicitly constrains MRP charging to protect the General Fund's ability to sustain core services, treating this as a binding constraint on debt repayment.
findings.matters: A lender should understand that the council's housing programme is material enough to warrant bespoke financing treatment and that protecting core service liquidity is being actively managed against housing scheme debt servicing.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: MRP will be charged at the maximum level up to the annuity level calculation that can be afforded from the Housing Reserve without undermining the Council's financial resilience, liquidity, or the sustainability of the General Fund and core service provision.

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 2A
findings.headline: Housing development MRP can be deferred to prevent the Housing Reserve from being depleted to zero
findings.detail: The council is adopting a new scheme-specific annuity method for housing coming into use in 2026/27 onwards. Crucially, it allows MRP charges to be deferred or reduced in initial years if needed to ensure the Housing Reserve does not deplete completely. MRP will be charged 'at the maximum level up to the annuity level calculation that can be afforded from the Housing Reserve' while protecting the General Fund and core services.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that housing schemes are forecast to strain the Housing Reserve enough that MRP deferrals are necessary to prevent full depletion—a concrete signal of early-years cash flow pressure and reserve vulnerability on this programme.
findings.figures: None provided in this extract
findings.quote: In the initial years of operation, the application of the annuity-based MRP charge may be deferred or reduced where necessary to ensure that the Housing Reserve maintains a sufficient forecast balance and is not depleted to zero.

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 1
findings.headline: Interest rate assumptions set at 4% long-term, suggesting environment risk above current rates
findings.detail: The council has adopted a 4% long-term borrowing assumption for property investment appraisals "to ensure that schemes remain viable even if interest rates rise above current levels." This prudent assumption indicates awareness that current rates may not hold and that 4% has been treated as a stressed scenario.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand whether 4% is adequate as a stress test for a portfolio with £704.8M of outstanding borrowing, and what happens to affordability if rates exceed this assumption.
findings.figures: 4% long-term borrowing assumption
findings.quote: In order to ensure that business cases remain robust against future movements in interest rates, a long term borrowing assumption of 4% will be used. This reflects a prudent long-term view of borrowing costs and ensures that schemes remain viable even if interest rates rise above current levels.

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 1
findings.headline: Council relying on refinancing of short-term loans exposes it to interest rate and liquidity risk
findings.detail: The council is borrowing below its liability benchmark by £451.9M in 2026/27, choosing short-term loans over long-term fixed borrowing. This creates refinancing risk as loans mature. While the document states this is mitigated by access to PWLB and local authority borrowing markets, refinancing £451.9M over coming years in a higher-rate environment could materially increase costs.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand whether the council can reliably refinance maturing debt and what interest rate assumptions underlie affordability projections.
findings.figures: £451.9M gap between gross borrowing (£662.7M) and liability benchmark (£681.8M) in 2026/27
findings.quote: This strategy should maintain a lower cost of borrowing through the financing of short-term loans but does show the refinancing risk this introduces the Council to. This risk is mitigated by the Council's ongoing access to the PWLB, and the liquid short term local authority to local authority borrowing market, allowing access to refinance borrowing as it becomes repayable.

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 1
findings.headline: Financing costs consuming 120% of net revenue stream with no path to improvement
findings.detail: Annual financing costs (interest and MRP) are forecast at £19.4M against a net revenue stream of £16.2M in 2026/27, a ratio of 120%. This ratio deteriorates to 134% by 2027/28 and 138% by 2028/29. The council is spending more on debt servicing than it collects in council tax, rates and grants after financing.
findings.matters: This ratio signals that the council's debt burden is becoming structurally unsustainable relative to its revenue base, and worsening over the forecast period indicates no corrective action is in place.
findings.quote: Proportion of financing costs to net revenue stream 120%

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 1
findings.headline: Property investment income declining while financing costs rise, creating structural deficits
findings.detail: Table 11 reveals that in 2026/27 financing costs (£19.4M) will exceed investment income (£19.4M) by a margin that is worsening: a deficit of £21k in 2026/27, growing to £617k by 2027/28. The document explicitly states this is "predominantly due to the ongoing increase in interest costs and reductions in property income", with any shortfall funded from reserves.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned that the council's capital investment strategy is no longer self-financing and that increasing portions of annual income are needed to cover financing gaps, eating into reserves.
findings.figures: 2026/27 deficit £21k; 2027/28 deficit £617k; 2028/29 deficit £174k
findings.quote: This table shows a worsening position from 2026/27 which is predominantly due to the ongoing increase in interest costs and reductions in property income. Both of these are funded from reserve, either via the General Fund or the Investment Property Reserve.

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 1
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement rising to £704.8M with accelerating trajectory
findings.detail: The cumulative outstanding borrowing (CFR) is forecast to rise from £649.2M in 2025/26 to £704.8M in 2026/27, and then to £770.9M in 2027/28 and £837.3M in 2028/29. This represents rapidly accumulating long-term debt.
findings.matters: The trajectory of total outstanding debt is material to credit risk and future financing capacity, particularly if interest rates remain elevated.
findings.quote: The Council's cumulative outstanding amount of borrowing is measured by the Capital Financing Requirement (CFR). This increases with new borrowing-financed capital expenditure and reduces with MRP and capital receipts used to repay borrowing. The CFR is expected to rise to £704M in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Capital, Treasury Management and Investment Strategy 2026-27 - App 1
findings.headline: Capital programme doubling to £109M with £62M (57%) financed by borrowing
findings.detail: Capital expenditure planned at £109.1M in 2026/27, up sharply from £48.9M forecast for 2025/26. Housing accounts for £102.3M of this. Borrowing is funding £62.4M of the programme, with only £31.9M from own resources and £14.7M from external sources.
findings.matters: A lender would need to assess whether this pace of borrowing-financed expansion is sustainable and whether the returns justify the risk.
findings.figures: £109.1M total capex, £62.4M borrowing (57%), £102.3M housing
findings.quote: In 2026/27 the Council is planning to incur capital expenditure of £109M

findings.paper_title: 25 Eastleigh Borough Council - Audit Results Report - 6 January 2026
findings.headline: Draft financial statements had quality control failures that should have been caught internally
findings.detail: Auditor reported that draft statements contained non-material internal inconsistencies, typographical errors, and arithmetic errors that should have been detected through internal quality review. A large number of disclosure misstatements were also identified.
findings.matters: Financial statement quality control failures suggest weakness in accounting function and increase audit complexity, cost and timeline.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: There were a number of non-material internal inconsistencies, typographical and arithmetic errors in the draft financial statements that should have been detected through internal quality review prior to publication.

findings.paper_title: 25 Eastleigh Borough Council - Audit Results Report - 6 January 2026
findings.headline: One Horton Heath development has ongoing governance and procurement risks
findings.detail: Auditor identified risk of significant weakness relating to governance and procurement for the One Horton Heath development. This was an identified risk from prior year audit and monitoring continued in 2024/25.
findings.matters: This is a major capital commitment (310 acres, 2,500 dwellings planned); governance issues could impact delivery and value recovery on council's significant investment.
findings.figures: 310-acre site; 381 properties first phase; 2,500 dwellings total outline planning permission
findings.quote: We identified a risk of significant weakness relating to the governance and procurement risks associated with the One Horton Heath development.

findings.paper_title: 25 Eastleigh Borough Council - Audit Results Report - 6 January 2026
findings.headline: Multiple material misstatements in asset valuations totalling millions
findings.detail: Auditor identified material misstatements across several asset categories: Property Plant & Equipment £1.8 million, DRC valuation £0.781 million, Nitrate Credits £0.8 million, One Horton Heath net overstatement £0.3 million. These suggest weakness in valuation controls.
findings.matters: Asset misstatements affect financial position; multiple errors across categories indicate control weaknesses in a key accounting process.
findings.figures: PPE £1.8m; DRC £0.781m; Nitrate Credits £0.8m; One Horton Heath £0.3m net overstatement
findings.quote: We have identified four misstatements totalling £1.8 million, understating Property, Plant and Equipment.

findings.paper_title: 25 Eastleigh Borough Council - Audit Results Report - 6 January 2026
findings.headline: Finance function lacks capacity to manage complexity of commercial activities and borrowing
findings.detail: Auditor identified risk of significant weakness in finance function capacity and expertise. This weakness relates to inability to manage the complexity of the council's commercial property and housing development activities and associated borrowing.
findings.matters: Finance function weakness directly impacts ability to manage complex operations, control risk, and service high levels of borrowing. This was an identified risk from prior year that monitoring continued in 2024/25.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: We identified a risk of significant weakness relating to the capacity and expertise within the finance function to identify, assess and manage risks to the Council's financial sustainability due to the complexity of the Council's commercial property and housing development activities and associated level and nature of borrowing.

findings.paper_title: 25 Eastleigh Borough Council - Audit Results Report - 6 January 2026
findings.headline: Council held £583 million borrowing under DLUHC debt moratorium for 9 months
findings.detail: As at 31 March 2024, council borrowing was £583 million (£440 million PWLB, £143 million short-term). DLUHC imposed a moratorium on new debt-funded investment in December 2023. The moratorium was lifted in December 2024 but government remains concerned about debt levels.
findings.matters: High debt creates financial risk; the moratorium and government concern about 'significant debt which is held by the Council and the risk which is carried with this' signals debt sustainability concerns.
findings.figures: £583 million total borrowing; £440 million PWLB; £143 million short-term
findings.quote: In December 2023 DLUHC issued a non-statutory Best Value Notice which stated the Council should 'Put in place a moratorium on new debt-funded asset investment'. This Best Value Notice was lifted in December 2024, however, it remained in place for 9 months of the financial year, and was lifted noting 'we still remain concerned about the significant debt which is held by the Council and the risk which is carried with this.'

findings.paper_title: 25 Eastleigh Borough Council - Audit Results Report - 6 January 2026
findings.headline: NNDR appeals provision materially overstated by £2.6 million
findings.detail: Two misstatements identified in the calculation: one factual and one judgemental. Both increased the provision beyond what should have been recorded, overstating liabilities.
findings.matters: Provision overstatement means reserves are actually lower than stated; this affects available resources to manage financial pressures.
findings.figures: £2.6 million total overstatement; £1.0 million council's share of the error
findings.quote: These two misstatements resulted in a total overstatement in the provision value of £2.6 million, of which the Council's share is £1.0 million.

findings.paper_title: 25 Eastleigh Borough Council - Audit Results Report - 6 January 2026
findings.headline: Auditor provides no assurance over short-term creditors — a major balance sheet item
findings.detail: Multiple misstatements were identified in the testing of creditors. The auditor is unable to conclude on completeness or accuracy of this significant balance and will modify the audit opinion to reflect this.
findings.matters: Creditors are a major liability; inability to verify them means total liabilities and liquidity position cannot be confirmed.
findings.figures: No specific figure disclosed, but noted as area where auditor cannot provide assurance
findings.quote: we are unable to conclude on the completeness or accuracy of the creditors balance held at 31 March 2024. As such, no assurance is provided over this balance

findings.paper_title: 25 Eastleigh Borough Council - Audit Results Report - 6 January 2026
findings.headline: Auditor will disclaim opinion on 2024/25 accounts, continuing pattern from three prior years
findings.detail: The auditor has not obtained sufficient evidence to provide reasonable assurance over in-year movements and closing balances. This continues disclaimers from 2021/22, 2022/23 and 2023/24. The lack of assurance over prior year balances and the backstop date mean the auditor anticipates a disclaimed 2024/25 opinion.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means the council's financial position cannot be independently verified by external audit, creating uncertainty for lenders about true financial standing.
findings.figures: Three consecutive prior-year disclaimers (2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24); 2024/25 also expected to be disclaimed
findings.quote: We therefore anticipate issuing a disclaimed 2024/25 audit opinion.
